title: Hammond firing Billie Holiday, and being told to growl on clarinet
summary: Hearing the story of Billie Holiday refusing to sing blues, Procope says Hammond thought Black singers had to sing blues; he recalls an arranger who asked him to growl on clarinet.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: Well, did you ever hear that John Hammond fired Billie from the Basie band because she wouldn't sing the blues?
Jo Jones told me that, and one night

at Jim and Andy's, he was a little high and he was talking on about that. And a few months later I was doing some research and I came across an old DownBeat from the '30s, and sure enough there was the whole story. She wanted to do, "I Can't Get Started," and he wanted her to do the blues, and she said, "I'm not a blues singer," and he said, "You're not Basie's singer either," and fired her.

Well, I suppose in that case, you see, and again this brings up the subject of, well, now, how can I put it? It brings up the subject of doing what you're told to do. Now, like I say, Fletcher Henderson's band were independent and outspoken, and Billie Holiday was independent and outspoken. Now, John Hammond, he thought that because she was a black singer she had to sing the blues. He wasn't ready to accept her as a singer. He thought Billie Holiday, the blues, that's it. And of course at that time Billie was in the mainstream of singers, and she wanted to sing the popular songs, which she could very well do, like everything else, and she could also sing, "Ain't Nobody's Business if I Do," as well as anybody else, too. And his scope wasn't broad enough to realize that, unless he just didn't want to realize it. He must have known it. That's what that was. I know, because I've been through that situation many times.
You know. Fletcher used to have all

sorts of arrangers, arranging his music, you know, and he had one guy, an arranger, came up to -- it was a rehearsal at Connie's Inn, and this arranger had written some notes on my part, you know, and he probably wanted me to play clarinet like Ted Lewis or somebody, but he said to me, "Well, can't you growl on it?" I said, "What do you mean, growl?" I said, "No, I can't growl on no clarinet." I probably could have done it, but I just wouldn't do it because he thought that that's what -- because you were a black musician, you know, you were supposed to growl on the clarinet. Not at all. Not at all. And that was the thinking in those days. That was the thinking. Everybody thought that way.
So I don't blame Billie Holliday one bit.
